domain_analysis.scope: Interior new construction trim stain and clear coat workflows for 7 trim profile types
domain_analysis.workflow_overview: Three-layer coating system: stain (color) → sanding sealer (adhesion bridge + smooth base) → clear topcoat (protection + depth). Each layer has distinct material systems and application techniques. coating_type dimension gates which layers are active.
key_differences_from_paint: Bare wood input (SS_BARE) instead of primed surface (SS_PRIMED_FIELD/SS_PRIMED_FACTORY)
No companion prime spec — stain spec handles all prep and all coating layers
Three product roles (stain, sealer, clear) instead of one (finish)
Independent application method selection for stain vs clear phases
Wipe step mandatory for all stain application methods
Wood conditioner activation for softwood species
Grain raise management for waterborne products on bare wood
User-selectable coat counts for all three layers with QT-driven defaults
No sheen/QT gate — all clear sheens available at all tiers
Stainable wood filler instead of paintable spackle for defect filling

workflow_phases.prep: Sand bare wood (120 → 150), fill defects with stainable wood filler, grain raise (conditional for WB), apply wood conditioner (conditional for softwood), tack clean
workflow_phases.apply: Stain coat(s) with wipe step, sanding sealer coat(s) with interstage sanding
workflow_phases.finish: Clear topcoat(s) with interstage sanding between
workflow_phases.interstage: Stain dry verification, sealer interstage sand (220-320), clear interstage sand (320-400)

required_paintscope_keys.description: Shadow box / picture frame molding linear footage
Wall masking LF at trim-to-wall edge

zones.notes: Drop cloth runners along trim perimeter. Stain drips harder to clean than paint — protection especially important.
Tape + paper masking at trim-to-wall edge. For stain work, also needed with brush when walls are finished — stain is difficult to remove from painted surfaces.
Spray only. Cover outlets/switches near spray zone.

analysis.interface_concern: Stain-to-paint wall interface. Stain is harder to clean from painted walls than paint is. Wall protection is critical when walls are finished.
analysis.protection_approach: Same masking as paint counterpart. Additional caution with stain — stain penetrates and cannot be wiped clean from painted surfaces.

analysis.interface_concern: Door casing often stained with same stain/clear as trim. May share session.
analysis.protection_approach: No protection needed when same finish. Routed to SF_DOOR_FRAME_NC_STAIN.

analysis.interface_concern: Crown molding meets ceiling. Clear coat drips on painted ceiling are difficult to remedy.
analysis.protection_approach: Light masking at crown-ceiling junction for spray. Brush method low risk.

state_analysis.notes: SS_BARE already exists. SS_STAINED and SS_CLEAR_COATED are new states per design spec Section 7.1. SS_CLEAR_COATED as input (recoating) is RP scope — excluded from this NC spec.

key_rates.stain_brush_wipe: 80 LF/hr — brush application with wipe. Slower than paint brush (also 80 LF/hr for coat 1) due to wipe step.
key_rates.stain_roll_wipe: 120 LF/hr — roll application with wipe. Faster application but includes wipe.
key_rates.stain_spray_wipe: 100 LF/hr — spray application with wipe. Faster spray offset by wipe step.
key_rates.clear_brush: 100 LF/hr — brush clear coat. Faster than stain brush (no wipe step).
key_rates.clear_spray: 150 LF/hr — spray clear coat. Production method.
key_rates.interstage_sand_400: 200 LF/hr — QT5 fine clear interstage sand.

production_rate_analysis.comparison_to_paint: Stain rates are generally comparable to paint rates for similar operations. Key difference: stain application includes wipe step (adds time), but stain requires no primer coat (saves a full layer). Net: stain_clear QT4 has more total coats (4 vs 2) but individual coat application is comparable speed.

risk_notes.risk: Softwood (pine, poplar, alder) absorbs stain unevenly, creating blotchy appearance
risk_notes.mitigation: Wood conditioner mandatory for softwood. Gel stain alternative (controls blotch without conditioner). Careful wipe technique.

risk_notes.risk: Water-based stain, sealer, or clear raises wood grain on bare wood, creating rough texture
risk_notes.mitigation: Grain-raise prep task: wet wipe bare wood, let dry, re-sand with 220 grit before first waterborne coat. Removes most grain raise issue.

risk_notes.risk: Rolling clear coat traps air bubbles that cure into visible defects
risk_notes.mitigation: Roll is PROHIBITED for clear coat application. Brush or spray only.

risk_notes.topic: Stain color inconsistency between trim types
risk_notes.risk: Different wood species, grain patterns, or application consistency across trim types creates color variation
risk_notes.mitigation: Use same stain lot. Consistent application technique (timing, pressure, wipe). Test on scrap first.

risk_notes.risk: Regular paintable spackle used for defect fill does not absorb stain — creates visible white spots
risk_notes.mitigation: STAINABLE wood filler only. Color-matched to final stain color when possible.

assumptions.value: New construction trim is bare, unfinished wood in good condition — no existing coatings, no damage beyond minor mill marks and nail holes
assumptions.note: RP stain specs (stripping existing finish) are out of scope for this NC spec.

assumptions.value: QT3: 1 stain + 0 sealer + 1 clear = 2 total. QT4: 1 stain + 1 sealer + 2 clear = 4 total. QT5: 1 stain + 2 sealer + 3 clear = 6 total. All user-overridable.
assumptions.note: No existing doctrine defines stain/sealer/clear coat count recommendations by QT. Derived from industry practice and design spec.

assumptions.value: No chemistry-pairing constraints between stain, sealer, and clear layers. Oil stain under WB clear is standard practice.
assumptions.note: Unlike paint specs where primer and finish should match chemistry, stain workflow has no such constraint.
